asDecan.p: Your Sun is in the first ten degrees of Pisces. The decans are ten-degree slices of a sign, and the Golden Dawn gave each one a ruling planet and one of the numbered cards, and yours went to Saturn. It's neither helped nor hindered in Pisces, so it takes its colour from the sign's ruler, Jupiter (Neptune, for modern astrologers). Pisces is mutable water, feeling that won't keep one shape for long, and Saturn is the planet of limits, clocks and hard decisions. With Saturn on the opening stretch, where the sign is at its freshest, the card is the Eight of Cups, someone who feels all of it and still gets up and goes. Jupiter's Nine, in the middle ten degrees, is far happier to stay put, and Mars closes the sign with the Ten. The Moon is your Sun card and covers all of Pisces. Saturn's own Major is The World, the card of a thing properly finished, and that's a large part of why a half-done ending bothers you so much.

You're usually the first to notice when something has gone flat. A dinner party is going well, the food's good, everyone's laughing, and somewhere around dessert you realise you'd quite like to leave, and you couldn't say why. A group chat you used to love starts to feel like homework, so you mute it, and six months later you've drifted out of it without a single argument. You can stay in a flat for years after it stopped feeling like home, because moving without a proper reason feels irresponsible to the Saturn part of you, and then one weekend you've signed a lease across town and everyone's surprised except you. On a Sunday with nothing planned you might clear out a wardrobe, get oddly teary over a jumper from ten years ago, and put it in the charity bag anyway.

You leave well, which is rarer than people think. When you finish a job you train your replacement properly and write the handover notes nobody else would bother with. When a relationship has run its course you tend to say so kindly, in person, so nobody's left guessing for months, and quite a few of your exes still send you a birthday message. Saturn in your slice also lets you put a dream on a timetable. Plenty of Pisces people carry a lovely idea for a book, a garden, a second career in music therapy, and it stays an idea for twenty years. You're more likely to be the one who gets up at six and writes for an hour before work, every weekday, for two years, and then actually sends the thing off.

Leaving can turn into your answer for everything. A friendship hits a rough patch and you just start replying a bit later each time. A choir or a club gets a new organiser you don't much like, and you simply stop turning up. Because you do it quietly and politely, nobody gets a chance to argue with you, and to be honest that's partly why you do it that way. The figure on your card has their back turned, and the eight cups behind them are all still standing, in perfectly good order. Sometimes what you walked away from only needed one awkward conversation or a bit of repair. The people left behind often say the same thing afterwards, that they had no idea anything was wrong, and they're usually telling the truth.

When something real goes wrong, a bereavement, a redundancy, months of being overlooked at work, the first thing you tend to do is go small and get organised. You tidy, you make lists, you cancel plans with a polite text, and you get very good at sounding fine on the phone. Saturn likes a routine when things fall apart. About a week in, the Pisces side comes up through the floor, often at an odd moment, crying in the supermarket car park or lying awake at three going over everything you might have done differently. The people close to you can feel shut out during the organised stage and then frightened by how low you get in the second one. What helps is someone checking in on a schedule, the same friend at the same time a few days a week, whether or not you say you're alright. Let them keep it up for a month, even once you're sleeping again.

You don't commit lightly, and once you do you treat it almost like a vow, which is Saturn talking. The part partners don't always understand is that you need to go off on your own now and then to stay in love. After an argument you might put your coat on and walk for an hour, and someone who doesn't know you well yet can read that as you leaving them. You're coming back. You just need some distance to work out what you actually feel. It helps to say that out loud early on, on a calm day, so they don't panic the first time the front door closes. You also keep score without saying so. You'll give up a lot for someone, weekends, a move interstate, and then years later it all comes out in one sentence during a fight about the bins.

You're good in jobs where something soft needs a firm frame around it. I see this decan running the volunteer roster at a hospice, editing other people's poetry, doing the timetable at a music school, and in pharmacy, social work and museum conservation. You can take in a lot of feeling from clients or patients and still get the paperwork in on time, and that combination is less common than it ought to be. The trouble is that you tend to outgrow roles quietly. You do a job well for three or four years, get the promotion, and then a flatness sets in that you can't explain to your manager, because nothing's actually wrong. Before you resign, try changing the job from the inside. Ask for a different project or a different team, or drop a day. Sometimes that's enough, and when it isn't you'll know properly.

In your twenties Saturn and Pisces tend to argue. You feel everything, Saturn tells you you're being too much, and you swing between drifting along and setting yourself very strict rules about how to live. A lot of early Pisces people leave things abruptly at that age, a course, a city, a relationship, and don't really understand why until later. By the mid-thirties there's usually been at least one departure you're proud of and one you regret, and between them they teach you a lot about when to go. You get slower to leave and clearer about your reasons when you do. The fifties often bring a settled seriousness about the things you love, music, faith, a craft, a cause, and you tend to give them real hours at last. I've seen a lot of people with this placement do their best work after fifty.

Every few months, take a sheet of paper and list the main things you give your time to: the job, each close friendship, the volunteering, the hobby you keep meaning to drop. Next to each one write a number from one to five for how much it still feeds you. Don't act on it. Keep the sheets, and after a year lay them out side by side. Some things will have been sliding for a long time and some only had a bad month, and the long slides are the ones to raise with someone, out loud, before you quietly let them go.
